reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story: Lena stood in her bedroom. She wanted her red boots. They were not here yet. "Yesterday we went to the store," said Mom. "You tried on the red boots. Do you remember?" Lena nodded. The store was loud and bright. Mom had said, "We will buy them tomorrow." Now it was today. But where were the boots? "The boots come soon," said Mom. "Soon?" asked Lena. What did soon mean? Was it a long, long wait? Lena looked at her old shoes. They were small. Her toes felt squished. She sat on her bed to wait. Mom read her one book. Then Mom brushed her hair. Then Lena heard the doorbell. It was Grandma! Grandma held a big bag. "Something is in here for you," she said. Lena peeked inside. The red boots! So that was soon. Soon was not long at all. Lena hugged Grandma. "Thank you, Grandma!" she said. She slipped the boots on, one, two. "Look at me!" said Lena. "Now let me stomp."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Athena put on her red boots. It was snowy at the park. Snow fell on her brown mittens. "Snow, snow, snow," she said.

"I want to keep some snow," said Athena. She rolled a little snowball. It was round and white. "I will put it in my glass cup."

The wind blew. It was windy, and her hat flew off. "I will hold my hat," she said. Papa picked it up.

At home, the house was warm. Athena put the snowball in her glass cup. "Now it is safe," she said.

She played with her blocks. She looked at the cup. The snowball was small. Then it was gone. A little puddle sat in the cup. "My snow turned to water," said Athena. Papa smiled. "Snow melts inside where it is warm," said Athena. "Next time I will keep it outside."

Papa hugged her. "Let's look out the window," he said. Outside, the snow would grow deep all night. Athena waved at the white park. "Bye bye, snow," she said. "See you tomorrow."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Aubrey sat at the dinner table. She had one big spoon. She had two little cups. Daddy put three peas on her plate. Aubrey poked them with her spoon. "Peas are round," she said.

Then her big brother Ben came in. He was smiling big. "I am seven today!" he said. He held up his fingers to show Daddy. Aubrey peeked at his hands. Seven was lots of fingers.

"How old are you, Aubrey?" Mommy asked. Aubrey looked at her own hand. She held up some fingers. "I am five!" she said. Ben laughed so hard his milk went slosh. "No, silly. Five is me, next year. You are three." Aubrey put down some fingers. Three fingers stayed up. "I am three," she said. Her voice felt upset for a minute, but then she grinned.

"Three peas for a three-year-old," said Daddy. He counted them out. "One, two, three." Aubrey ate them one by one. Then she held up her three little fingers again. "Three!" she said, and banged her spoon like a drum.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Charlie sat in her reading nook. She had letter cards all over the soft rug. Her cat, Socks, lay near her like a gray feather pillow. Charlie wanted to put the cards in a row. But she did not know where M went.

Dad sat close by with a warm mug. He did not pour tea on her cards, so she was not worried about spills. Charlie held the M card. "I am stuck," she said. Dad said, "Try your song."

Charlie sang the alphabet song. She sang slowly. A, B, C, D, E, F, G. She kept going. L came, and then M. M went after L. She put the card down in its spot. "It fits," she said. Socks woke up and yawned a stinky yawn. Charlie laughed and sang the song again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Ava and her family were going on a long drive. They were going to the beach to see Grandma. Ava sat in her car seat. She looked out the window.

After a while, Ava said, "I need the potty." Mom said, "Don't worry. We can stop soon." The car turned off the big road. It stopped at a rest stop. Ava asked, "Can we potty here?" Dad said, "Yes, that is what it is for." Ava held Mom's hand. They walked inside. Ava used the potty. Then she stretched her arms up high. Dad stretched too. They got back in the car.

Soon they saw the blue sea. Grandma waved from the sand. Ava dropped her short pink bucket by the water. The water came up. The bucket floated! Ava laughed and held Grandma's hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Ivy got a new library card. It had her name on it. She held it with both hands.

At the library, Ivy picked a book. It was about a worm in a garden. The worm dug in the dry dirt. "I want to keep this forever," Ivy said.

The librarian put a white paper in the book. "Bring the book back on this day," she said. She pointed to the white paper. That day was the due date.

At home, Ivy read the worm book. She read it in the morning. She read it after her nap. She read it three more times.

Then the due day came. Mom said, "Time to take the book back." Ivy hugged the book tight. "I don't want it to hurt to say goodbye," she said.

At the library, Ivy set the book on the desk. Then she saw a boy. He took her worm book. He sat down to read it. His smile grew big.

Ivy picked a new book to take home. The librarian stamped the white paper. "See you on the due date," she said.

Ivy grinned and held her card up high.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Raphael held his daddy's hand. They walked into the pool changing room. The floor was wet and shiny. Raphael could smell the water. He could hear kids splashing far away.

Raphael let go and started to run. His feet slid. He sat down with a bump. "Ouch," he said. Daddy helped him up fast. "The floor is wet," said Daddy. "Let's walk."

Raphael looked at his feet. He took one slow step. Then another. No sliding now. "Daddy, can I run to the pool?" he asked. "No," said Daddy. "We walk to the pool. Then we can play."

They walked all the way. Raphael held his towel tight. At the door, a big splash went boom. Water jumped over the edge. Raphael laughed. "A swimming game!" he said. Daddy held his hand. "Ready," said Daddy. "One, two, three, splash."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Sofia sat at the big table. She had a bag of letter cards. Mama sat next to her.

Sofia put the cards in a line. "A," she said. "B, C, D." She went on and on. "L, M, N, O, P." Then she stopped. "That is all," she said. "P is the last letter."

Mama smiled. "Let's sing the song," she said. They sang it slowly. They sang it again. After P came more sounds. Q, R, S, T. Sofia clapped. "Keep going," said Mama.

They sang to the end. "X, Y, Z," sang Sofia. "Now I know my A B Cs." She looked at her line of cards. P was not last. Z was last. She found the Z card in the bag. She put it at the end of the line.

Sofia touched each card. "A first," she said. "Z last." She picked up the bag. "Let's do it again," she said. Mama laughed and sang.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Aaron stood in the pool changing room with his dad. He pulled on his swim pants. Then he sat on the big bench to wait. "Will the water be too big for me?" he asked. "The teacher will help you," said Dad.

The pool room had a painting on the wall. It was a huge picture of a blue sea. Aaron looked at it while they walked to the water. Miss Kim the teacher smiled at him.

"Now we float on our backs," she said. Aaron felt scared. The water looked so wide. Miss Kim put her hands under his back. Aaron lay down on top of the water. Her hands held him up. "I'm floating!" said Aaron. "My tummy goes up and down with the waves." He kicked one foot and a splash hit Dad's nose. Dad laughed and said, "You are a real swimmer now."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Liam looked out the window. The sun was gone. The sky was gray. "Rain," said Mom. Big drops hit the glass. Tap, tap, tap.

"I want to go to the park," said Liam. "Not in the rain. My hair will get wet." Mom held up something red. It was the umbrella. She pushed it open. It went pop. "Put on your boots," said Mom. Liam pulled them on. They had ducks on them.

Outside, the wind blew. The tree waved its leaves. Mom held the umbrella over them both. Liam listened. The rain went tap, tap on the red top. But his hair stayed dry. He put out one hand. That hand got wet. He pulled it back under. "Dry again," he said.

"Is it snowy today?" Liam asked. "No," said Mom. "Snow is white and soft. Today is just rainy." They walked to the end of the street and back. At the door, Mom shook the umbrella. Drops fell off. Liam drank his juice by the window. The rain kept tapping. His hair was dry and straight, all the way home.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Sara ran to the pretend kitchen at the playground. It had a little orange pot and a little orange spoon. "I will make soup," she said. She stirred one potato, two carrots, three beans. A boy named Ben came to play too. "I am the baby," he said, and he sat in a small chair.

Sara fed the baby soup. "More, please," said Ben. The sun began to go down. Sara's mom called, "Time to go home soon."

Sara looked at the kitchen. It was a big mess. The pot was on the floor. The cup was under the bench. "We can't leave it like this," said Ben. Sara picked up the pot. Ben found the cup. They put back the spoon, the potato, the carrots, the beans. One, two, three, all done.

"Now the kitchen looks tidy," said Sara. She took one last look at the clean little kitchen. "Good night, kitchen," she whispered. Then she ran to her mom and held her hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Emilia went to the library with Dad. She wanted a book about a sleepy bear. She found a book with a bear on it. She opened it at the back. The pages went the wrong way. The bear was already in bed.

"No, no, sleepy bear," said Emilia. She turned the book around. She found the front. The bear woke up on page one. She patted the floor. "Sit here, book," she said.

"Who made up this bear?" she asked the librarian. The librarian pointed to the cover. "This name is the author," she said. "The author wrote the words."

Emilia looked at the name. She read the letters out loud, one by one. The author wrote the words. The words made the story.

She hugged the book. "You made my bear," she said to the name.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Amelia ran to the play kitchen at daycare. Her friend Ben was there too. He held a big red pot. "Soup!" he said. "Pinecone soup!"

Amelia peeked into the pot. She saw pinecones and paper leaves. She stirred with a big wooden spoon. Round and round the spoon went. "It's ready!" said Ben.

Amelia lifted the spoon to her mouth. She wanted to taste it. "Stop," said Miss Kim. "That soup is pretend." Amelia looked at the pinecones. Pinecones were not real food. Real soup came from the real kitchen. This soup was for pretending.

So Amelia opened her mouth wide. She made a big slurpy sound. "Sluuurp!" she said. She did not eat anything at all. Ben laughed and slurped too. The baby doll got a pretend spoon next. Amelia patted the doll's arm. "All gone," she said. "More soup tomorrow."

Ben clapped his hands. "Best soup ever!" he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Clara was at school. It was cold outside. "Brrr," said Clara. Everyone put on mittens.

Miss Kim gave out scarves. Clara got a red scarf. It was long. It went down to her shoes. Sam got a blue scarf. His scarf was short. It sat on his shoulders.

Clara tried to walk in her long scarf. She stepped on it. Plop! She fell down softly on the mat. "My scarf is too long," said Clara. Sam laughed. "That is a silly joke, scarf," he said. Clara laughed too.

Then Clara had an idea. She wrapped the scarf around and around her neck. Now it was short, just like Sam's. "Look, Miss Kim!" said Clara. "Now we match." Miss Kim smiled. "Good thinking, Clara," she said.

It was time to go outside. Clara ran fast to the door. Sam walked slow. Outside, the wind blew. Clara's scarf flapped like a red wing. Sam's scarf stayed snug. Miss Kim swept the snow off the steps with a big broom. Clara helped push the snow with her boot. A naughty gust of wind tugged at Sam's hat. Sam grabbed it just in time.

"Ready?" said Sam. "Ready," said Clara. They stepped out into the snow together.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Lucy wanted to sort her crayons by color. She made a red pile, a yellow pile and a green pile. Then she held up a dark blue crayon. "Where do you go?" she asked it. She put it in the blue pile.

Then she found a light blue crayon, the color of the sky. "Are you blue too?" she asked. "You look so pale!" She put it next to the dark blue one. They did not match. But they were both still blue. "Two blues," said Lucy. "Hello, blue family!"

She ran to get her doll. "Look, Dolly, light blue socks," said Lucy. She pointed at the doll's dark blue dress. "And this is dark blue. You wear two blues, Dolly!" Her big brother Sam peeked in. "That one is navy," he said, pointing at the dress. "Navy is dark blue," said Lucy. Sam laughed. "Okay, okay. You win."

They lined up all the blue crayons on the rug. Lightest first, darkest last. One, two, three, four, five, six. "It goes from sky to deep sea water," said Sam. Lucy clapped her hands. "Blue can be light. Blue can be dark. Blue is blue!" She picked up the lightest blue crayon and drew a big snow cloud, all white and pale. Sam drew deep dark waves under it. "Snow on top, deep blue below," he said. Lucy held up her drawing to show the doll. "Dolly, look! Our blue day!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Logan had a small violin. It was in a black case. He wanted to play it very much.

He opened the case. He took out the bow. He held it in his fist like a stick. He poked the violin with the tip. The violin made a squeak. "Oh no," said Logan. That sound was not pretty.

His big sister Mia came in. The cat ran to see too. "Can you help me?" asked Logan. "It is hard," said Mia. She sat down by him. She put the bow in his hand the soft way. "Now pull it across the strings," she said.

Logan pulled the bow across the strings. The violin sang. It went, "Looo!" Logan laughed. The cat's ears went up. "Again!" said Logan. He pulled the bow again. "Looo!" sang the violin.

Mia read her book while Logan played. He played to the cat. He played to Mia. The cat sat very still and listened.

"Play one more," said Mia. Logan pulled the bow, slow and smooth. "Looo," sang the violin, all the way to the end.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Aurora went to the dentist for the first time. The chair went up and down like a little ride. "Can I make it go?" she asked. The dentist smiled and said, "I will let you press the button." Aurora pressed it. The chair rose. She pressed it again. The chair came down.

Then a girl named Mia came in. She was young too. Mia picked up a toothbrush. "Oops," said Mia. "That one is Aurora's." Mia had grabbed the wrong one. Mia put it back and took her own toothbrush instead. Aurora looked at the two brushes. One was green. One was blue. Each brush had its own person.

"Where is my brush?" Aurora asked. The nurse pointed to the cup. "There it is, the green one." Aurora held it up. "Mine!" she said. The dentist laughed. "Yes, all yours." Aurora sat in the chair, opened her mouth wide, and let the little wheel spin and tickle her teeth.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story: Isabella painted a sun at school. It was high in the sky. She wanted to show it to her friend Mia. But Mia was not at school today. Mia was sick yesterday, too. Isabella felt sad. "I want to go now," she said. Her teacher said, "Mia is at her home. She lives near the park." Isabella put the painting in her bag. She would take it home after dinner. She would sleep in her bed. Then it would be tomorrow. Tomorrow is the day after today. So tomorrow, Isabella would wake up. She would get dressed. She would run to school with her painting. The next morning, Mia was there. Isabella held up the sun. Mia smiled big. "I love it," said Mia. "Let's paint one together now."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Leon was at Grandma's house. It was a snowy day. Snow fell past the big window. Leon wanted to bake bread for the whole family.

Grandma helped him mix flour and water. The dough felt sticky. It stuck to his fingers. "Oh no," said Leon. "Is it ruined?"

"Watch me," said Grandma. "Cooks push the dough and fold it." She pushed and folded. Then Leon tried it. He pushed the dough with his hands. He folded it over. The sticky bits came off his fingers. The dough turned smooth and soft.

"Did I do that?" asked Leon. "Yes, you did," said Grandma. She laughed at his happy noise.

Grandma put the bread in the hot oven. Leon stayed back and waited. Soon the bread was warm and golden. The family ate it together. Leon said, "I made this bread!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Gabriel went to the park with his dad. There was a little pond near the trees. Gabriel saw a fish swim by in the water. He waved at it. The fish swam away.

Dad brought two beanbags and a big red ball. "Let's play," said Dad. Gabriel wanted to toss a beanbag into the hoop. He threw it too low. It landed on the grass. He tried again, higher this time. The beanbag went in. "I did it!" said Gabriel.

Then Dad rolled the ball fast. Gabriel tried to catch it. It bumped his hands and fell. Dad said, "Let's try again." He tossed the ball slow and soft. Gabriel held out both hands. The ball came down gently. He caught it! Gabriel laughed. "Again!" he said.

A little girl came to play too. Gabriel rolled the ball to her, very softly. She caught it with both arms. "Silly ball," she said, and giggled. The sun went behind a cloud. They played until Dad called, "Time to go home." Gabriel waved to the fish in the pond.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Wyatt wanted a snack. Mom said, "You can have three grapes." Wyatt looked at the bowl. There were big grapes and small grapes. He picked three small ones. Then he saw the big grapes. Maybe big grapes counted less? He put the small grapes back. He took one big grape. That was only one grape on his plate. He took two more. One, two, three. He counted them with his finger. Three grapes sat on the plate. The big ones did not make more. Three still meant three.

Wyatt ate his grapes. They were sweet and cold. Then he saw a small bug on the window. "Mom, a bug!" he said. Mom came to look. Wyatt started to count the bug's legs. "One, two, three," he said. The bug crawled up. "Four, five, six." It went higher. "Seven, eight." Mom laughed. "Keep going," she said. "Nine, ten!" said Wyatt.

The bug found a little hole and went outside. "Bye, bug," said Wyatt. He waved at the window. "One bug," he said. "Ten legs." Mom gave him a kiss on his head. "One kiss," she said. Wyatt giggled. "Two!" he said, and kissed her back.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Elizabeth wanted to help sort the shopping. Mama put the bags on the floor. "Can I help?" asked Elizabeth. "Yes," said Mama. "You can sort."

Elizabeth made a pile of toys. She put the teddy bear in the pile. She put the ball in the pile. Then she held up a carrot. She put the carrot with the toys too.

Elizabeth looked at the carrot. She looked at the teddy bear. The teddy bear was soft. The carrot was hard and orange. Then she looked at the table. There sat an apple. There sat the bread. Mama was eating the apple. Papa was cutting the bread with a safe knife.

Elizabeth picked up the carrot. She carried it to the table. She set it down next to the apple. "Is this right?" she asked. "Yes," said Mama. "Good sorting, Elizabeth."

"Snack time," said Papa. He gave Elizabeth a small piece of apple. Elizabeth took a gentle bite. Then she gave the carrot a little kiss, just to say hello. Outside, a truck rolled down the street. Elizabeth waved at it and took another bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Alexander walked into the music classroom. A big guitar sat on a little red chair. "Can I play it?" he asked. Miss Rosa smiled. "Yes, you may try."

Alexander pulled the strings with his fingers. Plunk, plunk. He made a face. "It sounds funny," he said. "It does not sound like your guitar." Miss Rosa had a guitar too. Her strings made a nice sound.

Miss Rosa sat next to him. She turned the little pegs at the top of the guitar. She turned one, then another. "Now try again," she said. Alexander pulled the strings once more. The sound came out sweet and clear.

"It sounds good now!" said Alexander. He played a slow song. Miss Rosa tapped her foot along. On the wall, a poster showed a pig playing a violin. Alexander laughed. "Pigs can't play violins," he said. "But if one did, it would have to tune it too." He pulled the strings one more time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Jake stood in the backyard. The sun was warm on his face. He wanted to play hide and seek with Mama.

"Close your eyes," said Mama. Jake covered his eyes with his hands. "I see nothing," he said.

Jake peeked through his fingers. "I see the tree! I see the ball!" He opened his hands wide. Now he saw the flowers too.

"Eyes are for seeing," said Jake. "That is one sense!"

Then he heard a bird. "Ears are for hearing," he said. He sniffed the flowers. "My nose smells them!"

Jake touched the grass. "Fingers feel soft things," he said. Then he ate a nice snack. "My mouth tastes the apple!" He wiped his hands on a towel.

"Five senses," said Jake. "I said them all!"

"Yes you did," said Mama. She clapped her hands. "Now count to ten and find me!"

Jake closed his eyes and began. "One, two, three..."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Matthew went to the store with Mama. He wanted to buy apples for snack time. Mama said, "We need four apples." Matthew counted, "One, two..." Then he stopped. What came next? He could not remember.

A girl walked by with her daddy. She was singing a song. "One, two, buckle my shoe." Matthew listened. The song went on. "Three, four, shut the door." Matthew tapped his toes. The words felt bouncy in his ears. Did the song help him count?

He tried it himself. "One, two, buckle my shoe," he sang. Then he said, "Three! Four!" He looked up at Mama. "Mama, I know what comes after two!" Mama smiled. "Let's hear you count, Matthew."

He put apples in the bag. "One, two, three, four." The apples went plunk, plunk, plunk, plunk. The bag felt heavy and warm from his hands. The store lamp made a bright circle on the floor. Matthew stepped into the light. "Five, six, seven," he sang. What if he kept going?

"Eight, nine, ten," said the singing girl, passing by again. Matthew waved. "Ten! Big hen!" The girl laughed. At home, Mama cut the apples at the counter. Matthew sat safe at his little table. He sang his new song to the apples. "One, two, buckle my shoe." Then he took a big, crunchy bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Aurora sat on the big clean rug. Everyone was watching the game on TV. Dad was there. Grandma was there. Mr. Lee from next door was there too.

A man on TV threw a ball at a hoop. The ball went through the hoop. The crowd made a big happy sound. Aurora clapped her hands. "The ball went in the hoop," she said. She wanted to try that.

She ran to her toy bin. She found her soft red ball. She could not reach the real hoop. So she found something else. Her laundry bag hung on the door hook. It had a round open top, like a hoop.

Aurora stood back. She threw the ball. It hit the wall. She picked it up and tried again. The ball went into the bag. Dad clapped. Grandma clapped. Mr. Lee laughed a happy laugh.

Aurora bowed. Then she stirred her arms in a big circle like a slow wave. "More popcorn, please," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Elijah sat in his reading nook. He held a big letter card. The letter was S. It looked like a little snake.

"Can you find the S sound?" Mama asked. "It goes sss, like a hiss." Elijah listened. Sss. The sound tickled his ears a little.

He looked around the nook. Sun came in the window. "Sun!" he said. "Sss-un!" Mama smiled and nodded. Elijah put the card next to the sunny spot on the floor.

Next he saw his sock on the rug. He picked it up. "Sock starts with sss too!" The sock was sticky from his snack. He wiped his hands on his shirt and laughed.

Then he saw his sand pail by the door. "Sand! Sss-and!" He held up the card again. Sun, sock, sand. All three began the same way. All three made the hissing sound.

Elijah looked for more. He found a spoon in his toy box. "Sss-poon!" he said. Mama clapped her hands. Elijah hugged his letter card and whispered, "Sss."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Ellie went to the library with Dad. There was a big game on the rug. "Put things in piles," said the librarian. "Animals here. Toys here. Foods here."

Ellie found a stuffed dog. It was soft and brown. She put it in the animal pile. Then she stopped. She looked at the dog. She patted its fur. It did not wag. It did not bark. It was not alive. So it was a toy! Ellie moved it to the toy pile. "Good try," said the librarian. "You fixed it all by yourself."

Next Ellie found a cat, a ball, and an apple. "One cat, two toys, three foods," she said. The cat went in the animal pile. The ball went in the toy pile. The apple went in the food pile. She counted again. "One, two, three!"

Then Ellie found a little pillow. It was soft like the dog. She put it in the toy pile too. Now the dog sat on the pillow. It looked cozy. Ellie yawned. She was getting sleepy. "Close your eyes for one minute," said Dad with a smile. Ellie gave the sleepy toy dog one more pat. "Night night, little dog."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Ella wanted to read her new book all by herself. She sat on her bed and held it up. But she had it the wrong way round. The pictures looked funny. The bear came before the honey. The rain came before the clouds. "That is all mixed up," said Ella.

She turned the book over. Now the bear was on the front. She opened the front cover. She turned one page. Then another page. The bear found the honey at last. The cloudy sky came first, and then came the rain. "Is this the right way?" asked Ella. "Yes, it is," she said.

Some words sat under the pictures. Ella did not know them yet. She put her finger on them. She moved her finger, slow and careful, from left to right. Then she brushed her hand over the page, soft like paint on paper. "Words say something," said Ella. She turned the page to see what came next.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Maeva went to the big Diwali festival with Mama and Papa. The street was full of colors. There were flowers and drums and sweet smells. Maeva carried a basket of small clay lamps called diyas.

"I want to help," she said. So she set the diyas in a slow, careful row along the step. But the lamps looked dark and plain. "Why don't they shine?" she asked. Mama smiled. "Watch Papa."

Papa had a spoon of oil. He poured a little into each lamp. Then he touched a match to the wick. One lamp glowed. Then the next one glowed. Then the whole row glowed! Maeva clapped her hands. The oil had made the lamps light up.

A tiny flame flickered near Maeva's fingers. "Careful, it's hot," Papa said. He moved the lamp a safe bit away. Maeva watched the little lights dance. The whole street began to shine, one lamp at a time.

"More lights!" Maeva said, pointing down the step. She slipped another diya into place. Papa filled it with oil. It glowed too. "Now it's bright," Maeva whispered, and she and Mama counted all the little flames together.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Luka ran to the park with Dad. Dad had a picnic basket. "Let's play a game," said Dad. "We will find our five senses." Luka clapped his hands.

First, Luka closed his eyes. He heard a tiny bird. "I used my ears!" said Luka. Then he saw a big rainbow over the trees. "I used my eyes!" Next, he touched the warm slide. "I used my hands!" Then he sniffed an apple. "I used my nose!"

"Now the last one," said Dad. He held up a lemon slice. Luka licked it with his tongue. "Sour!" said Luka. His whole face scrunched up. Dad laughed. Then Luka chewed a sweet strawberry. "Yum! Sweet!" said Luka. "My tongue did that!"

"So what is the fifth sense?" asked Dad. "Tasting!" said Luka. "And my tongue does it!" Dad gave him a thumbs up. Luka licked the strawberry juice off his fingers and ran to the swings.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Athena sat under a big tree at the park. She had a bag of blocks with her snack. She tipped the blocks onto the grass. "I will sort them," she said. She put all the red blocks in one pile. Then she put all the blue blocks in another pile. Soon every block was in a pile by color.

Her friend Milo came to play. "Can I sort too?" he asked. Milo put the big blocks in one pile. Then he put the small blocks in another pile. Athena looked and looked. Same blocks, different piles! "They can go both ways," she said. She laughed and clapped her hands.

Milo found something round in the grass. It was a pinecone. Athena put it with the small pile. "It fits here," she said. Then she opened her snack bag. Apple slices and crackers came out. She gave some crackers to Milo. A leaf fell from the tree and landed on the big pile. Athena smiled and let it float down onto her knee. "Snack time," said Milo, munching happily.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Abigail wanted to draw a cat on the tablet. The screen was dark. She tapped it. Nothing happened. She tapped again and again.

Her teacher, Miss Kim, came over. "Press the round button on the side," said Miss Kim. Abigail pressed it. The screen lit up. It was bright and ready.

Abigail opened the drawing app. She drew a cat with a long tail. Then she drew wings so the cat could fly over a tree. "Look, Miss Kim! My cat can fly!" she said.

The bell rang. It was time for snacks. Abigail pressed the round button again. The screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the shelf, all by itself, next to a book about a tree with one big root.

"Thank you, Abigail," said Miss Kim. Abigail smiled and ran to the snack table.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Penelope loved water day at daycare. Teacher Mia let everyone splash in the little tub. First the kids took off their shoes and socks. Then they rolled up their pants. Penelope splashed and splashed until her arms were all wet.

Tommy jumped out of the tub and ran away. Drip, drip, drip went his feet on the floor. "Slip, slip!" he laughed. But then he got cold. He came running back for the big blue towel. He rubbed his arms and his legs. The towel made him dry and warm.

Penelope wanted to try that too. She stepped out of the tub, all drippy. "Towel, please!" she said. Teacher Mia gave her a soft yellow one. Penelope rubbed her arms. The drips went away. After that, everyone got dressed again. It was snack time. "Wet feet, dry feet, apple feet!" said Tommy. Penelope giggled and took a big bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Charlie stood by the big red gate. It was her first day of school. She held her mama's hand tight. The playground had swings and a slide. A boy ran past her fast. A girl laughed on the swings. Charlie looked around. Her tummy felt funny. She needed to find the bathroom. She did not know where it was.

She looked at the tall teacher. The teacher had yellow shoes. Charlie took one step. Then she took one more step. "Excuse me," she said. "Where is the bathroom?" The teacher smiled big. "Come with me," she said. "It is right inside." The teacher held out her hand.

Charlie took it. They walked past a poster of a silly worm wearing a hat. "The sun would melt that worm," Charlie said. The teacher laughed. They found the bathroom door. It had a blue sign. Charlie washed her hands after. Then she ran out to the slide. The teacher waved from the door.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Felix sat at the paint table at school. He wanted to make a card for Grandma. On the card he would paint a pink flower, big and round. But there was no pink paint on the table.

He looked and looked. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. There was green paint. There was white paint too. No pink anywhere. Felix felt like crying. "No pink, no pink," he said.

His teacher sat down next to him. "You can mix paints here," she said. Felix dipped his brush in the red. He made a red dot on his paper. Then he dipped his brush in the white. He stirred the white into the red dot. Round and round the brush went. He was a little scared to look. Then he peeked. The dot was pink! "Pink!" shouted Felix. "I made pink!"

He painted one big pink flower. Then he painted a yellow sun. He painted green grass and a blue sky. He held the card up high. "This is for Grandma," he said. "I hope she loves pink." He ran to show his teacher the pink flower first.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Ava sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. "Are we almost there?" she asked. "Almost," said Dad. "We are going to see your cousin Ben."

Ava had a job to do. She had a box on her lap. It was for Ben's new toy box. Ava looked inside. She found her red ball. She found her doll named Lucy. She found her blue blocks. "Ball, you go in," said Ava. She dropped it in the box. "Doll, you go in too." The doll went in. Then the blocks went in, one by one. They made a little click sound.

Ava saw the box was getting full. The ball made room for the doll. The doll made room for the blocks. When all the toys were in, the box was just right. Ava gave the box a pat. Then she saw her sock at the bottom of her bag. She held it up. "A sock is not a toy," said Ava. She put the sock back. Outside the window, a cow stood by a fence. "Moo," said Ava. The cow looked at her. Dad laughed. "A cow is not a toy either," said Ava. The car turned into Ben's street. Ben was waiting at the door, waving. Ava hugged the box tight. "I brought toys," she said. "So many toys."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Gianna stood at the airport. She held a big sign. It said "Grandpa!" People walked and walked. Then she saw him. "Grandpa!" she yelled. He gave her a hug.

At home, Grandpa took out a card game. "My turn first," said Gianna. She put down a card. Then she put down another. "My turn again!" Grandpa smiled. "Now it is my turn," he said. He put down one card. Then he pointed to her. "Now you." Gianna put down one card. Then Grandpa put down one. One for her, one for him, one for her, one for him. The cards made a funny long line. The line grew and grew!

"Grandpa, the cards make a train," said Gianna. "Choo choo!" Grandpa laughed. He turned over the last card. It had a red fish on it. "Oh no," said Gianna. "The fish ate the caboose!" Grandpa clapped his hands. "Good one," he said. "Same game tomorrow?" Gianna jumped up and down. "First turn is mine, then yours!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Elizabeth put on her new coat. It had no zipper. It had five red buttons.

She pulled the coat shut. The sides fell open again. She pulled them shut. They fell open again. Her friend Tom began to laugh. Elizabeth laughed too.

Teacher Mia sat down next to her. She held the coat still. Elizabeth looked at the little holes. She pushed a button through a hole. Pop. The button went in. The coat stayed shut on that side. Elizabeth's eyes got big. She pushed the next button through its hole. Pop. Two sides closed now.

She pushed and pushed. One button slipped away. She tried again, slow this time. Pop. At last all five buttons were in. The coat was closed and warm.

Tom showed his big tooth in a smile. "Let's go out," he said. Elizabeth ran to the door. She was fast in her red coat.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Madelyn had a party dress. It was red and shiny. "I wish to wear it all night," she said. She twirled in front of the mirror.

But the dress was scratchy at bedtime. It poked her arms. It rode up when she sat. "Hmm," said Madelyn. "Can a dress sleep?" She looked at her bed. She looked at her dress. What could she wear to sleep?

Then she saw her pajamas. They were soft and warm. They had wild bears on them. She touched the pajamas. So cozy! Madelyn put on the pajamas all by herself. Off went the dress. On went the bears.

Madelyn climbed into bed. She snuggled down. The pajamas were warm. Her teddy was warm too. "Good night, bears," she said. The bears did not answer. They were sleeping, just like her.
